intro: Toronto built the tallest freestanding structure on Earth to fix bad television reception. This is how a broadcast antenna became Canada's defining silhouette.
page_title: CN Tower: Exploded 3D Model and History | Architectural Atlas

sections.body: In the early 1970s, Toronto's skyscraper boom created an unexpected problem: the new towers blocked broadcast signals and reception across the city turned to static. Canadian National, the railway company that owned prime downtown land, proposed the blunt solution: build one tower taller than everything else and put every antenna on it. Architects John Andrews, Webb Zerafa and Menkes Housden drew a 553.3-meter concrete needle. Construction started on 6 February 1973 at a budgeted cost of CA$63 million, on the former Railway Lands at what is now 290 Bremner Boulevard.
sections.heading: A tower to clear the static

sections.body: The shaft went up by slip-forming: concrete poured continuously into a climbing mold, 24 hours a day, for 40 months, using more than 40,000 cubic meters of concrete. The tower topped out on 2 April 1975, and the antenna sections were hoisted into place by helicopter, then the world's most powerful. When it opened to the public on 26 June 1976, with the official ceremony on 1 October, the CN Tower was the tallest freestanding structure in the world, a title it held until 2007. The completed structure weighs about 130,000 tons and sways up to two meters at the antenna in high wind, exactly as designed.
sections.heading: Poured in one go

sections.body: The main pod holds seven storeys of attractions. The Glass Floor opened on 26 June 1994 at 342 meters: 2.5-inch-thick panels of layered glass and air, each load-tested every year. Above it sit the LookOut level at 346 meters and the 360 Restaurant at 351 meters, revolving once every 72 minutes. Higher still, the SkyPod at 447 meters is one of the highest public observation decks in the world. In 2011 the tower added the EdgeWalk: a hands-free walk around a 1.5-meter-wide ledge on the pod roof at 356 meters, harnessed to an overhead rail. The 1,776-step stairwell opens twice a year for charity climbs.
sections.heading: Seven storeys in the sky

sections.body: For 31 years the CN Tower was the tallest freestanding structure on the planet, and it remains the tallest in the Western Hemisphere. In 1995 the American Society of Civil Engineers named it one of the Seven Wonders of the Modern World. About 1.5 million people ride its elevators every year at 6 meters per second. It has survived lightning strikes, ice storms and the city's entire condo boom without losing its place on the skyline: the exclamation point at the end of Toronto.
sections.heading: The world's tallest, then an icon

sections.body:
Toronto's film industry keeps putting the tower on screen, sometimes on purpose and sometimes by accident. Edgar Wright's Scott Pilgrim vs. the World (2010), the most proudly Toronto of blockbusters, opens its title sequence on a shot where the CN Tower takes up most of the screen. David Cronenberg's Videodrome (1983) lets it loom in background shots like a silent sentinel, which suits a film about sinister broadcasts. The F Word (2013) frames it behind Riverdale Park in its east-end romance.

And then there is the giveaway problem. Toronto so often stands in for other cities that locals play spot-the-landmark as a sport: The Incredible Hulk (2008) dressed Yonge and Dundas as Harlem for its climax, but the skyline kept betraying the location. The tower is the tell. When a supposedly anonymous downtown suddenly grows a 553-meter concrete needle, the audience knows exactly which city they are looking at.
